The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of female Peloponnesos barbel was assessed from specimens collected during the peak spawning period. Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the gonadosomatic index was 12% [GSI = 12%]. This index was derived from gravid individuals sampled during the late spring months, when ovarian development reaches its maximum. This pattern is consistent with the life history strategy of a small-bodied cyprinid inhabiting resource-limited freshwater systems. The measurements were performed on freshly sacrificed specimens, with ovaries excised and weighed to the nearest 0.001 gram before fixation. The thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] was maintained throughout the acclimation period of 14 days prior to sampling, ensuring that the observed gonadal state reflected standard metabolic conditions for this population during the reproductive window.

A separate series of field measurements conducted across multiple drainage basins in the Peloponnese provided estimates of key somatic endpoints for Barbus peloponnesius. The ultimate total length, representing the maximum standard length recorded in this dataset, was 19 centimeters [Li = 19 centimeters], a value that corresponds closely to the upper size limit reported for the species in ichthyological surveys of the region. This length is notably smaller than that of its congener Barbus balcanicus, underscoring the comparatively diminutive body plan of the Peloponnesos barbel. In a related analysis focused on reproductive maturation, the total length at puberty for females was estimated at 6 centimeters [Lp = 6 centimeters], a threshold derived from histological examination of gonadal tissue that revealed the onset of vitellogenesis at this size. This finding was further corroborated by length-frequency histograms showing the first appearance of actively spawning females at this approximate body length. The convergence of these two metrics provides a robust framework for constructing size-based maturation schedules applicable to population modeling efforts. All length measurements were recorded to the nearest 0.1 centimeter using digital calipers on fresh specimens prior to preservation.

Early life history parameters for the Peloponnesos barbel were derived from incubation experiments using fertilized eggs obtained from wild-caught broodstock. The wet weight at birth, calculated from the average egg diameter of 1.888 millimeters using the formula for a prolate spheroid, was determined to be 0.0035 grams per individual [Wwb = 0.0035 grams per individual]. This initial mass reflects the relatively small volume of yolk reserves available to the developing embryo, a trait that necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding after eclosion. The yolk-sac larvae emerged approximately 96 hours post-fertilization when incubated at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a temperature that accelerates metabolic processes and shortens the endotrophic phase compared to cooler regimes. The endogenous yolk reserves are consumed within the first 72 hours after hatching, after which the prolarvae must commence active feeding on microzooplankton to sustain growth. This early life stage is characterized by high mortality rates in natural environments, as the small initial body mass leaves the larvae vulnerable to starvation and predation. The estimated egg volume and resulting birth mass are consistent with values published for other small-bodied Barbus species inhabiting similar thermal niches.

The allometric relationship between length and mass in Barbus peloponnesius was evaluated using a power-law regression fitted to a sample of 230 adult specimens. From this relationship, the ultimate wet weight was determined to be 64.7 grams [Wwi = 64.7 grams] for individuals attaining the maximum length of 19 centimeters. This mass-length scaling coefficient is typical of benthic cyprinids with a fusiform body shape and moderate condition factor. In the same dataset, the wet weight at puberty associated with the 6 centimeter length threshold for females was calculated as 2.9 grams [Wwp = 2.9 grams], representing the body mass at which reproductive maturation is first anatomically detectable. This relatively low mass at maturation suggests that the species allocates a substantial portion of its early growth toward reaching the size threshold for reproduction rather than accumulating large somatic reserves beforehand. The contrast between the 2.9 gram pubertal mass and the 64.7 gram asymptotic adult mass indicates that post-maturation growth remains significant, with females continuing to increase in body size across multiple spawning seasons. This pattern is consistent with an iteroparous life history strategy where fecundity scales positively with maternal body size, favoring delayed senescence and repeated reproductive events.

Longevity estimates for Barbus peloponnesius were derived from mark-recapture studies conducted over a five-year field period in the Evrotas River system. The maximum lifespan was determined to be 18 years, or approximately 6570 days [am = approximately 6570 days], when assessed under the prevailing thermal conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This lifespan is notably extended for a cyprinid of this body size and suggests a relatively slow pace of life, with delayed senescence and sustained reproductive output well into advanced age. The recapture data indicated that individuals older than 12 years still exhibited active gonadal development and participated in annual spawning migrations. The thermal dependence of this longevity estimate is critical, as metabolic rate and cellular maintenance costs are temperature-sensitive; at the 25 °C [T = 25 °C] regime typical of the species' lowland habitats during the active season, the observed lifespan represents a balance between metabolic acceleration and the cumulative effects of oxidative stress. Comparative data from populations inhabiting cooler headwater streams suggest that lifespan may be further extended under lower thermal regimens, though this remains to be systematically quantified. The 6570 day maximum confirms the species as one of the longer-lived members of the Barbus genus in European freshwaters.
